historical_timeline.summary: Born near what is now Hodgenville, Kentucky.
Kicked by a horse and briefly appeared lifeless.
Mother died of milk sickness when he was nine.
Older sister died from complications during delivery.
Described himself as "the most miserable man living" in a letter to John T. Stuart.
Son Eddie died after a long illness.
Son Willie died in the White House, probably of typhoid fever.
Illness after the Gettysburg Address, retrospectively interpreted as smallpox.
Died the morning after being mortally wounded at Ford’s Theatre.

claims.statement: Abraham Lincoln was born February 12, 1809, near what is now Hodgenville, Kentucky.
Lincoln was mortally wounded at Ford’s Theatre on the night of April 14, 1865, and died at the Petersen House at 7:22 a.m. on April 15, 1865, aged 56.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: In 1859 Lincoln described himself as "six feet, four inches, nearly" in height.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Informs the synthetic height measurement; the measurement itself remains S.

claims.statement: In his tenth year Lincoln was kicked by a horse and, in his own account, "apparently killed for a time."
claims.clinical_interpretation: A documented childhood injury; no modern head-injury diagnosis is inferred.

claims.statement: On January 23, 1841, Lincoln wrote to John T. Stuart, "I am now the most miserable man living."
claims.clinical_interpretation: A contemporaneous first-person description of severe low mood.

claims.statement: Lincoln’s recurrent melancholy is retrospectively interpreted by modern clinicians as chronic depression that did not prevent him from leading the nation.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The modern label is retrospective; the low mood is separately documented in his own words.

claims.statement: Lincoln’s mother, Nancy Hanks Lincoln, died of milk sickness on October 5, 1818, when he was nine.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Milk sickness was poisoning from milk of cows that ate white snakeroot.

claims.statement: Marfan syndrome, or another inherited marfanoid disorder such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B, has been proposed retrospectively from Lincoln’s build; the diagnosis is disputed and has never been genetically confirmed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Keep as a contested historical hypothesis; do not place on the active problem list.

source_links.locator: Cited as the first Marfan proposal; full text not reviewed
Abstract: proposes a marfanoid disorder and MEN2B rather than classic Marfan syndrome

claims.statement: Lincoln’s older sister, Sarah Lincoln Grigsby, died on January 20, 1828, at age twenty-one, from complications during delivery that also took her infant’s life.
Lincoln’s son Edward ("Eddie") died on February 1, 1850, after a long illness, at three years and ten months.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The NPS chronology says the illness was probably tuberculosis.

claims.statement: Lincoln’s son William ("Willie") died in the White House on February 20, 1862, probably of typhoid fever, at age eleven.

Lincoln’s November 1863 illness after the Gettysburg Address has been retrospectively interpreted as unmodified smallpox, more serious than his physicians reported publicly; the interpretation is disputed.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Lincoln returns six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg daily for a moderate depressive episode. His mood is brighter on most days, and he is enjoying his work again. He is back at court on his usual schedule and writes letters to friends two or three times a week. He falls asleep within half an hour and wakes once a night, compared with the broken sleep he described at intake, and his concentration on long briefs is better. Mild nausea in the first two weeks settled by the third week. He has had no headache, diarrhea, restlessness, or sexual side effects. He misses about one dose every two weeks. He has had no suicidal thoughts since the intake visit and still carries his safety plan. He drinks no alcohol. He saw Dr. Natarajan of psychiatry this morning.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Lincoln is a 32-year-old man with major depressive disorder, single episode, in early remission on sertraline 50 mg daily (PHQ-9 4 nine days ago), who asked for a same-day visit. Three days ago he spent an afternoon in shorts and a short-sleeved shirt clearing overgrown brush and vines at a friend's property. The next morning itchy red streaks appeared on both forearms, then blisters, spreading over two days to the backs of both hands, the right side of his neck, and both shins. The itch woke him repeatedly on the last two nights, and he worries that the poor sleep means his depression is coming back. He says his mood itself is unchanged and he has had no suicidal thoughts. Calamine lotion and cool showers help briefly. He has not yet washed the clothes or gloves he wore. He has no fever, eye swelling, genital involvement, or trouble breathing, and he has never had a stomach ulcer.

assessment_plan.assessment: Classic linear vesicles after brush clearing, over about 20 percent of the body surface and including both hands. At this extent topical steroids alone are not enough, so a systemic course is indicated, tapered over two to three weeks because a short course or dose pack often lets the rash rebound. There is no sign of secondary infection

hpi.narrative: Mr. Lincoln returns for an adult preventive visit, four weeks after his twelve-week depression review. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit. The poison ivy rash cleared during the prednisone taper, which he finished four days ago, with no rebound. He slept more lightly on the first three nights of the 60 mg dose but had no mood change, racing thoughts, or irritability, and the nurse telephone check four days into the course found the rash improving and his sleep back to normal. His mood has stayed good, his PHQ-9 is 3 today, and he has had no suicidal thoughts. He continues sertraline 50 mg daily and misses about one dose every two weeks. He walks most evenings and is working full days.

referral.question: Moderate major depressive disorder, single episode, in a 32-year-old attorney starting sertraline 50 mg daily. Please confirm the diagnosis, look for bipolar spectrum illness, review his suicide risk and safety plan, and advise on medication management and psychotherapy
referral.urgency: Routine; booked for the day of his six-week review. No current suicidal ideation
referral.pertinent_history: Low mood, loss of interest, and poor sleep over several weeks are affecting his legal work and friendships, with reduced concentration and missed work. PHQ-9 14. No current suicidal ideation, intent, or plan; access to lethal means reviewed; collaborative safety plan with crisis resources, including the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, completed today. Protective factors: close friendships, a sense of purpose in public service, and engagement in treatment. No earlier depressive episode is documented. His mother died when he was nine and his older sister in his late teens. No tobacco or alcohol use; no known allergy. Sertraline 50 mg daily started today after shared decision-making; he prefers medication to psychotherapy
questions: Do you agree with the diagnosis of a single, moderate, uncomplicated episode of major depressive disorder, and is there any sign of bipolar spectrum illness or another condition that would change treatment?
Is sertraline 50 mg daily an appropriate first choice, and when should the dose be increased?
Please review his suicide risk and the collaborative safety plan.
Would you add psychotherapy, and how long should treatment continue after remission?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Lincoln is seen at the request of Dr. Marquez six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg daily for a depressive episode with low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, and poor concentration. His mood is brighter on most days, he is back at court on his usual schedule, and he writes to friends again. He falls asleep within half an hour and wakes once a night. Mild nausea settled by the third week; he has had no restlessness, agitation, or sexual side effects, and he misses about one dose every two weeks. He describes no past periods of elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, or unusual risk-taking, and no hallucinations or unusual beliefs. He uses no alcohol, tobacco, or other drugs. He has had no suicidal thoughts since the intake visit and carries his safety plan. No prior suicidal behavior is recorded. He lost his mother at nine and his older sister in his late teens, and he spoke about those losses without current preoccupation. He prefers to continue medication alone for now
consultant_note.data_reviewed: PHQ-9 14 at intake and 9 today; the intake safety assessment and collaborative safety plan; today's vital signs; the medication list. No laboratory tests are on record, and none are needed for sertraline

No hallucinations

assessment.assessment: Diagnosis confirmed. The episode is uncomplicated: no psychotic features, no substance use, and no earlier episode on record. The PHQ-9 has fallen from 14 to 9 in six weeks, a 36 percent reduction: a partial response that is still improving on a well-tolerated starting dose
Not suspected. There is no history of hypomanic or manic symptoms and no activation on sertraline. No Mood Disorder Questionnaire was done at intake; after this interview it adds little now

Acute risk is low: no ideation, intent, plan, or preparatory behavior; access to lethal means has been reviewed; he is engaged in care and has strong protective factors in his friendships and his sense of purpose. The active depressive episode keeps risk above his baseline until remission. The collaborative safety plan is appropriate, and outpatient care is the right setting

recommendations: Continue sertraline 50 mg daily; he is improving steadily and tolerating it well
Increase to 100 mg if the PHQ-9 is not below 5 at the twelve-week review
PHQ-9 at least monthly until remission, so a nurse telephone check in about four weeks, then every two to four weeks in the continuation phase
Reassess suicide risk at every visit with the C-SSRS Since Last Visit or PHQ-9 item 9, and keep the safety plan current; 988 at any time
After remission, continue sertraline at the dose that achieved it for at least six months, then taper gradually with his clinician rather than stopping suddenly

Psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral or interpersonal therapy) is a reasonable addition but not required for an uncomplicated episode. He prefers medication alone, and the guideline supports monotherapy; offer it again if his response stalls or he relapses
No laboratory monitoring is needed for sertraline. Avoid regular NSAIDs and other serotonergic drugs such as tramadol, triptans, St John's wort, and dextromethorphan without checking first
Reassess for bipolar disorder, using the Mood Disorder Questionnaire, if elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, or racing thoughts appear
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Marquez in person today; the patient agrees with the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Primary care will continue measurement-based care on the CMID schedule. Psychiatry will see him again if the PHQ-9 has not halved after a dose increase, for any suicidal ideation, or for features of bipolar disorder
